\title{Trained Conditional Flows Memorise\\
at an Effective Bandwidth}

\author{Anonymous authors \\ Paper under double-blind review}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
With the training set fixed, the population minimiser of conditional flow matching
sends a condition that identifies one example to that example, and Gaussian noise on
the condition turns its endpoint into a Nadaraya--Watson mixture of the training atoms.
We show that trained networks follow this mixture (at image scale, its mean and total
variance) at one \emph{effective bandwidth}
$h_{\mathrm{eff}}$, fitted to their per-condition variances and recovered independently
from their per-condition means (48/48 synthetic and 31/36 CIFAR-10 checkpoints), which
training shrinks towards the bandwidth $h$ of the label noise. We prove when
$h_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is identified and what calibration it implies: for any prior, label
noise moves the coverage of the reference law by at most a total-variation term of
order $\sqrt{k}\,h^2/\sigma^2$, and a vanishing effective sample collapses it to zero.
From $h_{\mathrm{eff}}$ the theorem predicts the held-out coverage of 75 trained
synthetic checkpoints with $R^2=0.90$, ranking it better than the training loss or the
iteration; at image scale the sample spread ranks it better.
\end{abstract}

% ==========================================================================
\section{Introduction}

Flow matching \citep{lipman2023flow,albergo2023building,liu2023rectified} regresses a
velocity field on a path from noise to data. Used for posterior sampling, conditional
flow matching is calibrated early in training and then becomes nearly deterministic,
returning training examples \citep{physicscfm2026}. That the empirical minimiser
memorises is known for unconditional models
\citep{gao2024flow,bertrand2025closed,kamb2024creativity,buchanan2025edge,li2026memory}.
We ask what the \emph{conditional} minimiser does, what the usual fix, Gaussian noise on
the condition \citep{ho2022cascaded,sadat2024cads}, buys, and how far a trained network
is from either (Figure~\ref{fig:mechanism}). Our contributions:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt]
\item \textbf{An exact reference.} A condition that identifies its example is sent to it;
  label noise at bandwidth $h$ gives a Nadaraya--Watson (NW) mixture of the training
  atoms, atomic at every $h$ (Section~\ref{sec:theory}).
\item \textbf{One number per checkpoint.} A trained network follows that mixture at one
  bandwidth $h_{\mathrm{eff}}$ (at image scale, in its mean and total variance),
  identified by two disjoint statistics; we prove when it
  is identified (Section~\ref{sec:heff}).
\item \textbf{A calibration theorem.} The bandwidth sets the coverage of credible
  regions, for any prior, and predicts the measured coverage of trained synthetic models
  (Section~\ref{sec:calib}).
\end{itemize}

\section{The exact reference}
\label{sec:theory}

Fix $\D=\{(x^i,y^i)\}_{i=1}^N$, $x^i\in\R^d$, with distinct labels $y^i\in\R^k$, as in
inverse problems and inpainting. Draw $I\sim\mathrm{Unif}\{1,\dots,N\}$,
$X_0\sim\pi_0=\N(0,I_d)$, $t\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$, $\eps\sim\N(0,I_k)$; set
$X_t=(1-t)X_0+tx^I$, $U=x^I-X_0$, $\widetilde Y=y^I+h\eps$, and minimise
$\E|U-v(X_t,t,\widetilde Y)|^2$; the minimiser is $\vstar=\E[U\mid X_t,t,\widetilde Y]$.
Write $K_h(u)\propto e^{-|u|^2/2h^2}$ and $p_i^{(h)}(y)=K_h(y-y^i)/\sum_jK_h(y-y^j)$.

\begin{theorem}[Endpoint law]
\label{thm:endpoint}
At $h=0$, $v_0^\star(x,t,y^i)=(x^i-x)/(1-t)$, the loss is zero and every source point
reaches $x^i$. For $h>0$ the flow of $\vstar$ from $\pi_0$ ends at
$p_1(\cdot\mid y)=\sum_ip_i^{(h)}(y)\,\delta_{x^i}$, with moments
$\bar x_h(y)=\sum_ip_i^{(h)}x^i$ and $\Covh(y)=\sum_ip_i^{(h)}(x^i-\bar x_h)(x^i-\bar
x_h)^\top$. It is supported on the atoms at every $h$, so if the posterior gives the
atoms no mass, $W_2^2(p_1,p(\cdot\mid y))\ge\int\dist(x,\{x^i\})^2p(x\mid y)\,dx>0$,
independently of $h$. \proofin{}
\end{theorem}

So label noise matches the posterior's variance at best, never its law. Noise on the
interpolant changes nothing and only noise on the endpoint leaves the atoms
(Appendix~\ref{app:interventions}).

% ==========================================================================
\section{Trained models sit at an effective bandwidth}
\label{sec:heff}

A trained model need not sit at its own training bandwidth. With $T_c$ and $m_c$ its
generated trace and mean at condition $y_c$,
\begin{equation}
h_{\mathrm{eff}}=\arg\min_{h'}\sum_c\big(\log T_c-\log\tr\mathrm{Cov}_{h'}(y_c)\big)^2,
\qquad
h_{\mathrm{mean}}=\arg\min_{h'}\sum_c\big\|m_c-\bar x_{h'}(y_c)\big\|.
\label{eq:heff}
\end{equation}
The two use disjoint statistics, so $h_{\mathrm{mean}}\approx h_{\mathrm{eff}}$ checks
that the model is a mixture over the training atoms at all; other atomic references pass
that check too, the Gaussian one wins on fit quality, and a non-atomic spread around
each atom does not improve it (Table~\ref{tab:families}).

\begin{proposition}[Identifiability]
\label{prop:heffid}
With $D_i=|y-y^i|^2$ and $\Cov_p$ the covariance over $i$ under $p^{(h)}(y)$,
$\partial_h\bar x_h=h^{-3}\Cov_p(x^i,D_i)$ and
$\partial_h\tr\Covh=h^{-3}\Cov_p(|x^i-\bar x_h|^2,D_i)$, so the latter is $O(h^{-3})$ as
$h\to\infty$. Let $F(h)=(\log\tr\mathrm{Cov}_h(y_c))_c$, the measured log traces be
$F(h_{\mathrm{true}})+e$, and $\hat h$ minimise $|\log T-F(h)|$ over a set
$\mathcal H\ni h_{\mathrm{true}}$. Then $\hat h\in\{h\in\mathcal
H:|F(h)-F(h_{\mathrm{true}})|\le2|e|\}$; if this set lies in an interval $\mathcal I\ni
h_{\mathrm{true}}$ on which $u\cdot F'\ge\kappa>0$ for a unit vector $u$, then $|\hat
h-h_{\mathrm{true}}|\le2|e|/\kappa$. \proofin{}
\end{proposition}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_heff_synthetic.png}
\caption{Linear-Gaussian problem, three seeds per bandwidth. (a) $h_{\mathrm{eff}}$
falls with training and stops just above the training bandwidth $h$ (dashed); line:
geometric mean over seeds, band: range. Checkpoints before 3000 iterations, where no
bandwidth fits, are omitted. (b) The bandwidth fitted to the variances against the one
implied by the means, with 95\% bootstrap intervals: two disjoint statistics give one
bandwidth (Table~\ref{tab:families} for other reference families). Open markers ($h=0.5$): the reference barely varies and
$h_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is poorly identified.}
\label{fig:heffsyn}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Results.} On a linear-Gaussian problem ($d{=}2$, $N{=}200$; 15 MLP runs,
$h\in\{0,0.01,0.05,0.1,0.5\}$) the two bandwidths agree within 95\% intervals at all
48 checkpoints where the reference varies; $h_{\mathrm{eff}}$ falls between $10^4$ and
$10^5$ iterations and settles at $1.08h$. At $h{=}0.5$ it is poorly identified, as the
proposition predicts ($\kappa$ is $1.4$ there against $5$--$33$ for $h\le0.1$). With a
$35.75$M-parameter DDPM U-Net on CIFAR-10 inpainting ($N{=}2000$, six runs,
$h\in\{4,5\}$) they agree at 31/36 checkpoints, and $h_{\mathrm{eff}}$ falls to
$1.13$--$1.34h$ by 60k iterations (Figure~\ref{fig:heffsyn}; CIFAR-10 in
Figure~\ref{fig:heffcifar}, appendix).

\section{The bandwidth sets calibration}
\label{sec:calib}

\begin{theorem}[Calibration of the reference law]
\label{thm:calib}
Let $X\sim\pi$, $Y=g(X)+\eta$, $\eta\sim\N(0,\sigma^2I_k)$, with $\pi$, $g$ arbitrary,
and $\pi_h(\cdot\mid y)$ the law of $X$ given $Y+h\eps=y$.
(a) For an i.i.d.\ training set, $p_1(\cdot\mid y)\Rightarrow\pi_h(\cdot\mid y)$ as
$N\to\infty$. (b) Level-$\alpha$ regions of $\pi_h$ cover $X$ at the clean label $Y$
with probability within $\tau_h=\mathrm{TV}(\N(0,\sigma^2I),\N(0,(\sigma^2{+}h^2)I))
\le\sqrt{k/8}\,h^2/\sigma^2$ of $\alpha$; (c) if $\pi$ is Gaussian and $g$ linear, at
least $\alpha$. (d) A region built from $n_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/\sum_iw_i^2$ weighted atoms
has expected covariance $(1-1/n_{\mathrm{eff}})S$; at $n_{\mathrm{eff}}=1$ it covers
with probability $0$. \proofin{}
\end{theorem}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\textwidth]{fig_t3_coverage.png}
\vspace{-3pt}
\caption{Linear-Gaussian problem. (a) Coverage of the nominal 90\% region against
bandwidth: infinite-data limit (Theorem~\ref{thm:calib}c), over-covering for $h>0$;
finite effective sample (d), collapsing at small bandwidth; dots: 75 trained
checkpoints at their $h_{\mathrm{eff}}$. (b) Coverage predicted from $h_{\mathrm{eff}}$
against the measured coverage.}
\label{fig:t3}
\end{figure}

Parts (b, c) give the over-coverage edge of a calibration window, (d) the collapse edge.
Modelling the atoms near a held-out $y^\star$ as draws of $\pi_h$ with the actual
weights, (d) predicts the held-out 90\% coverage of all 75 synthetic checkpoints from
their $h_{\mathrm{eff}}$ with $R^2=0.90$, $[0.85,0.93]$ resampling runs
(Figure~\ref{fig:t3}). As a ranking,
$h_{\mathrm{eff}}$ (Spearman $0.92$) beats the training loss ($0.85$) and the iteration
($-0.41$), keeps $0.90$ with the iteration partialled out, and repeats on an eight-mode
mixture posterior ($0.91$; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}). On the mixture the
bound (b) holds and is nearly tight at $h=\sigma/2$.

\section{Limitations and conclusion}

Which bandwidth training reaches is measured, not proved: a kernel model of spectral bias
reproduces the fall of $h_{\mathrm{eff}}$ to $h$, and limited label resolution provably
reweights the atoms without moving them (Appendix~\ref{app:specbias}), but neither
explains why networks stop just above $h$. Calibration is shown where the posterior is
known ($d\le8$); at image scale $h_{\mathrm{eff}}$ fits the variances no better than a
power law, and the sample spread ranks held-out coverage better than $h_{\mathrm{eff}}$
does (Spearman $0.98$ against $0.63$). Within that scope, the bandwidth read off a
checkpoint places it relative to its training set and sets its calibration; extraction
is read from the on-atom fraction.

\label{endmain}

\appendix
\section{Proofs}
\label{app:proofs}

Throughout, conditionally on $I=i$ and for $t<1$ the map $X_0\mapsto X_t$ is an affine
bijection, so $p(x\mid I=i,t)=(1-t)^{-d}\pi_0\big(\tfrac{x-tx^i}{1-t}\big)>0$, and the
factor $(1-t)^{-d}$ cancels in every posterior over $I$. Every field below has the form
$\sum_iw_i(x,t)(x^i-x)/(1-t)$ with smooth weights in $[0,1]$ summing to one; it is
therefore locally Lipschitz on $\R^d\times[0,1)$ with $|v|\le(|x|+\max_i|x^i|)/(1-t)$,
so by Gr\"onwall each trajectory exists on $[0,1)$ and the push-forward of $\pi_0$ is the
unique solution of the continuity equation there \citep[Ch.~8]{ambrosio2008gradient}.

\paragraph{Projection.} For $m=\E[U\mid X_t,t,\widetilde Y]$,
$L_h(v)=\E|U-m|^2+\E|v-m|^2$, since the cross term vanishes by the tower property; so
$\vstar=m$ a.e.\ and $\inf_vL_h=\E\Var(U\mid X_t,t,\widetilde Y)$.

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:endpoint}, $h=0$]
Distinct labels give $I=i$ from $Y=y^i$, and then $X_0=(X_t-tx^i)/(1-t)$, so
$U=x^i-X_0=(x^i-X_t)/(1-t)$ is a function of the conditioning variables. Hence
$v_0^\star=(x^i-x)/(1-t)$ and $L_0(v_0^\star)=0$. Along
$\dot x_t=(x^i-x_t)/(1-t)$, $\frac{d}{dt}\frac{x_t-x^i}{1-t}=0$, so
$x_t=(1-t)x_0+tx^i\to x^i$ for every $x_0$, and $p_1=\delta_{x^i}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:endpoint}, $h>0$]
Given $I=i$, $X_t$ and $\widetilde Y$ are independent, so by Bayes
$\Pr(I=i\mid X_t=x,t,\widetilde Y=y)\propto\pi_0\big(\tfrac{x-tx^i}{1-t}\big)K_h(y-y^i)=:w_i$,
and $U=(x^i-x)/(1-t)$ given $I=i$, $X_t=x$; this gives the field. Now fix $y$ and
consider the coupling $J\sim p^{(h)}(y)$, $X_0\sim\pi_0$ independent, $X_1=x^J$,
$X_t=(1-t)X_0+tX_1$. Its index posterior is
$\propto p_i^{(h)}(y)\pi_0\big(\tfrac{x-tx^i}{1-t}\big)\propto w_i$, so
$\E[X_1-X_0\mid X_t=x,t]=\vstar(x,t,y)$. For $\varphi\in C_c^\infty$,
$\frac{d}{dt}\E\varphi(X_t)=\E\langle\nabla\varphi(X_t),X_1-X_0\rangle
=\E\langle\nabla\varphi(X_t),\vstar(X_t,t,y)\rangle$, so $\law(X_t)$ solves the
continuity equation of the flow from $\pi_0$ and, by uniqueness, equals the flow's
marginal. Since $X_t\to x^J$ almost surely, $p_1=\law(x^J)=\sum_ip_i^{(h)}(y)\delta_{x^i}$.
The moments follow. As $h\to0$ with a unique nearest label $i^\star$,
$K_h(y-y^i)/K_h(y-y^{i^\star})\to0$ for $i\ne i^\star$; as $h\to\infty$,
$p_i^{(h)}\to1/N$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the floor in Theorem~\ref{thm:endpoint}]
The support statement is the endpoint law. For any coupling $(X,X')$ of
$p_1(\cdot\mid y)$ and $p(\cdot\mid y)$, $X\in\{x^i\}$ almost surely, so
$\E|X-X'|^2\ge\E\dist(X',\{x^i\})^2=:F(y)$; take the infimum over couplings. $F$
involves only the atoms and the posterior, and is positive because the atoms are
$p(\cdot\mid y)$-null.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:interp}]
Given $I=i$, $r:=x-tx^i=(1-t)X_0+\gamma Z\sim\N(0,s_t^2I_d)$, so
$\E[X_0\mid r]=\frac{1-t}{s_t^2}r$ and $\E[Z\mid r]=\frac{\gamma}{s_t^2}r$. Hence
$v^\star_\sigma(x,t,y^i)=x^i+c(t)(x-tx^i)$ with
$c=\frac{-(1-t)+\gamma\dot\gamma}{s_t^2}=\frac12\frac{d}{dt}\log s_t^2$. Then
$u_t=x_t-tx^i$ solves $\dot u=c(t)u$, so $u_t=s_tx_0$ (as $s_0=1$). Finally
$s_t^2=(1-t)[(1-t)+\sigma^2t]$, so $s_1=0$ and $x_t\to x^i$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:endpointnoise}]
Given $I=i$, $r:=x-tx^i=(1-t)X_0+t\rho\xi\sim\N(0,s_t^2I_d)$ with
$s_t^2=(1-t)^2+t^2\rho^2$, so the index posterior is
$\propto\varphi_{s_t}(x-tx^i)K_h(y-y^i)$ and, by Gaussian conditioning,
$\E[U\mid X_t=x,t,I=i]=x^i+\frac{t\rho^2-(1-t)}{s_t^2}(x-tx^i)$. This field is smooth
on $\R^d\times[0,1]$ since $s_1=\rho>0$. The coupling $J\sim p^{(h)}(y)$,
$X_1=x^J+\rho\xi$ has the same index posterior and conditional velocity, so, as in the
proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:endpoint}, $p_1=\law(x^J+\rho\xi)=\sum_ip_i^{(h)}\N(x^i,\rho^2I_d)$,
with mean $\bar x_h$ and covariance $\Covh+\rho^2I_d$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:heffid}]
Fix $y$ and write $p_i=p_i^{(h)}(y)=e^{-D_i/2h^2}/Z$ with $Z=\sum_je^{-D_j/2h^2}$.
\emph{Derivatives.} $\partial_h\log e^{-D_i/2h^2}=D_i/h^3$ and
$\partial_h\log Z=\sum_jp_jD_j/h^3=:\bar D/h^3$, so
\begin{equation}
\partial_hp_i=p_i\,(D_i-\bar D)/h^3 .
\end{equation}
Hence for any $f$ not depending on $h$,
$\partial_h\sum_ip_if(x^i)=\sum_ip_i(D_i-\bar D)f(x^i)/h^3=\Cov_p(f(x^i),D_i)/h^3$. With
$f(x)=x$ this is the first identity. For the second,
$\tr\Covh=\sum_ip_i|x^i|^2-|\bar x_h|^2$, so
\begin{align*}
h^3\partial_h\tr\Covh
&=\Cov_p(|x^i|^2,D_i)-2\,\bar x_h\cdot\Cov_p(x^i,D_i)
=\Cov_p\big(|x^i|^2-2\bar x_h\cdot x^i+|\bar x_h|^2,\,D_i\big),
\end{align*}
since adding the constant $|\bar x_h|^2$ does not change a covariance, and the first
argument is $|x^i-\bar x_h|^2$.
\emph{Large $h$.} As $h\to\infty$, $p_i=1/N+O(h^{-2})$ uniformly in $i$, $\bar x_h\to\bar x$,
and both arguments of the covariance are bounded, so
$h^3\partial_h\tr\Covh\to\frac1N\sum_i(|x^i-\bar x|^2-m)(D_i-\bar D_\infty)$ with $m$ and
$\bar D_\infty$ the unweighted means; the error is $O(h^{-2})$.
\emph{Stability.} Write $h_\circ=h_{\mathrm{true}}\in\mathcal H$ (on a grid, replace $e$
by the misfit at the grid point nearest $h_\circ$). By optimality of $\hat h$,
$|F(\hat h)-F(h_\circ)-e|=|\log T-F(\hat h)|\le|\log T-F(h_\circ)|=|e|$, so
$|F(\hat h)-F(h_\circ)|\le2|e|$, which is the first claim. If that set lies in
$\mathcal I$, then $\hat h\in\mathcal I$, and by the mean-value theorem applied to
the scalar function $u\cdot F$ on the segment between $h_\circ$ and $\hat h$,
$|F(\hat h)-F(h_\circ)|\ge|u\cdot(F(\hat h)-F(h_\circ))|=|u\cdot F'(\xi)|\,|\hat h-h_\circ|
\ge\kappa|\hat h-h_\circ|$ for some $\xi\in\mathcal I$. Combining the two gives
$|\hat h-h_\circ|\le2|e|/\kappa$. The argument uses only that $\hat h$ minimises a
distance to a curve, so it applies verbatim to $h_{\mathrm{mean}}$ and $G$.
\end{proof}

In part (c) write $s_h^2=\sigma^2+h^2$, $\Sigma_h=(\Sigma_x^{-1}+A^\top A/s_h^2)^{-1}$, $\Gamma_h=\Sigma_hA^\top/s_h^2$ and $\mu_h(y)=\Sigma_h\Sigma_x^{-1}\mu_x+\Gamma_hy$ for the prior $\N(\mu_x,\Sigma_x)$ and $g(x)=Ax$; then $\pi_h(\cdot\mid y)=\N(\mu_h(y),\Sigma_h)$, and the claim of (c) is $X-\mu_h(Y)\sim\N(0,\Sigma_h-h^2\Gamma_h\Gamma_h^\top)$.

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:calib}]
\emph{(a)} Let $\widetilde Y=Y+h\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon\sim\N(0,I_k)$ independent;
given $X=x$, $\widetilde Y\sim\N(g(x),s_h^2I_k)$, so $\widetilde Y$ has the everywhere
positive density $p_{\widetilde Y}(y)=\E\,\N(y;g(X),s_h^2I_k)$. For a bounded continuous
$\varphi$, by Theorem~\ref{thm:endpoint},
\begin{equation*}
\int\varphi\,dp_1^{(h)}(\cdot\mid y)
=\frac{\frac1N\sum_iK_h(y-y^i)\varphi(x^i)}{\frac1N\sum_iK_h(y-y^i)}
\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}
\frac{\E[K_h(y-Y)\varphi(X)]}{\E[K_h(y-Y)]}
\end{equation*}
by the strong law of large numbers, since $K_h$ is bounded and the denominator's limit is
positive. Conditioning on $X$ and using $\int K_h(y-y')\N(y';g(x),\sigma^2I)\,dy'=
\N(y;g(x),s_h^2I)$, the numerator is $\E[\varphi(X)\N(y;g(X),s_h^2I)]
=p_{\widetilde Y}(y)\,\E[\varphi(X)\mid\widetilde Y=y]$ and the denominator is
$p_{\widetilde Y}(y)$. Taking $\varphi$ in a countable convergence-determining class gives
weak convergence almost surely.

\emph{(b)} Given $X=x$, $Y\sim\N(g(x),\sigma^2I_k)$ and $\widetilde Y\sim\N(g(x),s_h^2I_k)$,
so the total variation between the laws of $(X,Y)$ and $(X,\widetilde Y)$ is
$\E_X\,\mathrm{TV}(\N(g(X),\sigma^2I),\N(g(X),s_h^2I))=\tau_h$, by translation
invariance. The function $(x,y)\mapsto\ind\{x\in R(y)\}$ takes values in $[0,1]$, so its
expectations under the two laws differ by at most $\tau_h$. By Pinsker's inequality and
$\mathrm{KL}(\N(0,\sigma^2I_k)\,\|\,\N(0,s_h^2I_k))=\frac k2(r-1-\log r)$ with
$r=\sigma^2/s_h^2=1/(1+u)$, $u=h^2/\sigma^2$, we get $\tau_h^2\le\frac k4(r-1-\log r)
=\frac k4\big(\log(1+u)-\frac u{1+u}\big)\le\frac k8u^2$, the last step because the
bracket vanishes at $u=0$ and has derivative $u/(1+u)^2\le u$. Finally, if
$\pi_h(R(y)\mid y)=\alpha$ for every $y$, then
$\Pr(X\in R(\widetilde Y))=\E[\pi_h(R(\widetilde Y)\mid\widetilde Y)]=\alpha$.

\emph{(c)} $\widetilde Y=AX+\tilde\eta$ with $\tilde\eta\sim\N(0,s_h^2I_k)$, so Gaussian
conditioning gives $\pi_h(\cdot\mid y)=\N(\mu_h(y),\Sigma_h)$. $\mu_h$ is affine,
$\mu_h(\widetilde Y)-\mu_h(Y)=h\Gamma_h\varepsilon$, and
$X-\mu_h(\widetilde Y)\sim\N(0,\Sigma_h)$. Since $X-\mu_h(Y)$ is a function of $(X,\eta)$,
which is independent of $\varepsilon$,
\begin{equation*}
\Sigma_h=\Cov\big(X-\mu_h(Y)-h\Gamma_h\varepsilon\big)=\Cov\big(X-\mu_h(Y)\big)+h^2\Gamma_h\Gamma_h^\top,
\end{equation*}
and $X-\mu_h(Y)$ is Gaussian with mean $\E X-\mu_h(\E Y)=0$, which is the claim. Write
$z=\Sigma_h^{-1/2}(X-\mu_h(Y))\sim\N(0,I-h^2MM^\top)$ with
$M=\Sigma_h^{-1/2}\Gamma_h$. The eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ of $I-h^2MM^\top$ lie in $[0,1]$, so
$|z|^2\overset{d}{=}\sum_j\lambda_jg_j^2\le\sum_jg_j^2\sim\chi^2_d$ for i.i.d.\ standard
normal $g_j$, and $\Pr(|z|^2\le q_\alpha)\ge\Pr(\chi^2_d\le q_\alpha)=\alpha$. If $h>0$
and $A\ne0$ then $\Gamma_h\ne0$, some $\lambda_j<1$, the inequality between the two sums is
strict on an event of positive probability that intersects $\{\chi^2_d>q_\alpha\}$ with
positive probability, and the coverage is strictly larger than $\alpha$.

\emph{(d)} Let $a_i$ be i.i.d.\ with mean $m$ and covariance $S$ and $\sum_iw_i=1$. Then
$\Cov(\sum_iw_ia_i)=\sum_iw_i^2S=S/n_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and with $\bar a=\sum_iw_ia_i$,
\begin{equation*}
\E\sum_iw_i(a_i-\bar a)(a_i-\bar a)^\top
=\E\sum_iw_i(a_i-m)(a_i-m)^\top-\E(\bar a-m)(\bar a-m)^\top
=S-S/n_{\mathrm{eff}} .
\end{equation*}
If $n_{\mathrm{eff}}=1$, one weight is $1$, the weighted covariance is $0$, the region is
the single point $\bar a$, and an absolutely continuous $x^\star$ falls in it with
probability $0$.
\end{proof}

The numerical checks of every part are in \texttt{scripts/theory\_t1\_check.py},
\texttt{theory\_t3\_coverage.py} and \texttt{theory\_t3\_general.py}.

\section{Where noise enters}
\label{app:interventions}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}llll@{}}
\toprule
noise on & population endpoint law & effect & result\\
\midrule
interpolant, $\gamma(t)=\sigma\sqrt{t(1-t)}$ & $\delta_{x^i}$ for every $\sigma$ & none &
Prop.~\ref{prop:interp}\\
label, bandwidth $h$ & $\sum_ip_i^{(h)}\delta_{x^i}$ & reweights atoms &
Thm.~\ref{thm:endpoint}\\
endpoint, $X_1=x^I+\rho\xi$ & $\sum_ip_i^{(h)}\N(x^i,\rho^2I_d)$ & moves support,
$+\rho^2I_d$ & Prop.~\ref{prop:endpointnoise}\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Where noise enters, and what it does to the population endpoint law. Only
endpoint noise yields an absolutely continuous law, to which the floor of Theorem~\ref{thm:endpoint} does not
apply; it pays for continuity in variance.}
\label{tab:interventions}
\end{table}

\begin{proposition}[Interpolant noise]
\label{prop:interp}
Let $h=0$, $X_t=(1-t)X_0+tx^I+\gamma(t)Z$ with $Z\sim\N(0,I_d)$ and target
$\dot X_t=x^I-X_0+\dot\gamma(t)Z$. With $s_t^2=(1-t)^2+\gamma(t)^2$ the optimal flow is
$x_t=tx^i+s_tx_0$; since $s_1=0$, $p_1(\cdot\mid y^i)=\delta_{x^i}$ for every
$\sigma\ge0$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[Endpoint noise]
\label{prop:endpointnoise}
With $X_1=x^I+\rho\xi$, $\xi\sim\N(0,I_d)$ redrawn at every step and $h>0$, the endpoint
law is $\sum_ip_i^{(h)}(y)\N(x^i,\rho^2I_d)$, with mean $\bar x_h(y)$ and covariance
$\Covh(y)+\rho^2I_d$.
\end{proposition}

\paragraph{Which reference family.}
\label{app:families}
Agreement of $h_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and $h_{\mathrm{mean}}$ shows that the means and the
variances are explained by one member of the reference family. It does not show that
the family is the right one. We therefore refit the same samples (the 48 checkpoints of
Section~\ref{sec:heff}, $M{=}1000$ at 20 conditions) under five families, each with one
scale $s$ and the same estimator \eqref{eq:heff}. Four are mixtures over the training
atoms with weights $w_i\propto e^{-|y-y^i|^2/2s^2}$ (Gaussian, the reference of
Theorem~\ref{thm:endpoint}), $e^{-|y-y^i|/s}$ (Laplace), $(1+|y-y^i|^2/s^2)^{-1}$
(Cauchy), and uniform weights on the $s$ nearest labels (kNN). The fifth is not atomic:
the linear-Gaussian posterior with observation noise $s$, whose covariance does not
depend on $y$. The Gaussian family reproduces the published fit exactly (the same
$h_{\mathrm{eff}}$ at 120/120 checkpoints). A sixth family, also not atomic but with a
variance that depends on $y$, is the endpoint-smoothed law
$\sum_ip_i^{(s)}(y)\N(x^i,\rho^2I_d)$ that noise of scale $\rho$ on the training
endpoints produces at the optimum, with trace $\tr\mathrm{Cov}_s(y)+d\rho^2$; it nests
the Gaussian at $\rho=0$, so it is fitted over
$(s,\rho)$ and compared by leave-one-condition-out error, where the extra parameter
counts only if it predicts conditions it was not fitted to.

Interval agreement does not separate the families (Table~\ref{tab:families}): kNN passes
it at all 48 checkpoints and Laplace at 45. Fit quality does. Paired at each checkpoint,
the Gaussian reference has the lower variance misfit than Laplace at 36/48 checkpoints
and in 9/12 runs (median log-RMSE difference $0.020$, 95\% bootstrap interval $[0.011,
0.024]$), than Cauchy at 41/48 and than kNN at 48/48. Its variance-fitted scale also
predicts the means best at 41/48. The posterior family's $R^2=-0.12$ shows only that
the trained variance varies across conditions, which a $y$-independent covariance cannot
follow. The test that could fail is the endpoint-smoothed family, and it does not
displace the atoms: $\hat\rho=0$ lies inside its bootstrap interval at 41/48 checkpoints,
$d\hat\rho^2$ is at most $8\%$ of the trace, and its held-out error is lower than the
Gaussian's at 10/48 checkpoints and higher at 17. Only at $h{=}0$ does it help at half
the checkpoints, by a median $0.0007$ in log-RMSE. The evidence is therefore for a
mixture over the training atoms whose weights are best described by the Gaussian
kernel, with the Laplace kernel a close second. The preference is weakest where the
smoothing is the network's own: the Gaussian fits best at 7/12 checkpoints at $h{=}0$,
against 11/12 and 10/12 at $h=0.05$ and $0.1$, where it is also the kernel of the
training noise. At $h{=}0.5$, where the reference barely
varies, the Gaussian family still fits the variances best (14/15) but its intervals agree
at only 9/15, as Proposition~\ref{prop:heffid} predicts.

\section{Where the bandwidth comes from}
\label{app:specbias}


Proposition~\ref{prop:heffid} and Theorem~\ref{thm:calib} say when $h_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is
identified and what it implies, not why training produces it. We test the simplest
mechanism: a learner that resolves the label only gradually. The trained field depends
on $y$ through the conditional moments $f^\star(y)=\E[\phi(X)\mid\widetilde Y=y]$,
$\phi(x)\in\{x,|x|^2\}$, which at bandwidth $h$ are the Nadaraya--Watson moments of
Theorem~\ref{thm:endpoint}. Suppose they are learned by kernel gradient flow in
$L^2(\rho_h)$, $\rho_h$ the law of $\widetilde Y$, from the unconditional moments
$c=\E\phi(X)$:
\begin{equation}
\partial_tf_t=-T_k(f_t-f^\star),\quad f_0=c,
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
f_t=c+(I-e^{-tT_k})(f^\star-c),
\label{eq:kgf}
\end{equation}
with $(T_kg)(y)=\E_{\rho_h}[k(y,Z)g(Z)]$. This is
the linearised dynamics of a network whose dependence on $y$ is governed by a fixed
kernel $k$ \citep{jacot2018neural}, which learns low frequencies first
\citep{rahaman2019spectral}.

\begin{proposition}[Resolution under kernel gradient flow]
\label{prop:specbias}
(a) Let $h=0$ and $k$ be strictly positive definite on the distinct labels
$\{y^i\}$. Then at every condition $y^j$, $f_t(y^j)\to f^\star(y^j)$ exponentially fast,
so the model's mean tends to $x^j$ and its variance to $0$: it reaches the reference
at $h$, with no floor. (b) Let $\rho$ be Lebesgue measure on $\R$ (a uniform label
density) and $\hat k(\omega)=a|\omega|^{-\zeta}$. Then $f_t-c$ is $f^\star-c$ filtered by
$\hat\varphi_t(\omega)=G\big(\omega\,(at)^{-1/\zeta}\big)$, $G(u)=1-e^{-|u|^{-\zeta}}$: a
low-pass filter of fixed shape whose resolution scale is $s(t)=(at)^{-1/\zeta}$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
(a) $\rho_0$ is uniform on $N$ points, so $L^2(\rho_0)\cong\R^N$ and $T_k$ is the matrix
$K/N$, $K_{ij}=k(y^i,y^j)$, with $K$ positive definite and smallest eigenvalue
$\lambda_{\min}>0$, and self-adjoint for the uniform weights;
hence $\|f_t-f^\star\|\le e^{-t\lambda_{\min}/N}\|f^\star-c\|$ in $\R^N$, which bounds
every coordinate. At $y^j$ the hard-conditioning moments are $f^\star(y^j)=(x^j,|x^j|^2)$,
so the mean tends to $x^j$ and the variance $|x^j|^2-|x^j|^2=0$.
(b) With $\rho$ Lebesgue, $T_k$ is convolution with $k$, the Fourier multiplier
$\hat k(\omega)$, so $e^{-tT_k}$ is the multiplier $e^{-ta|\omega|^{-\zeta}}$ and
$I-e^{-tT_k}$ the multiplier
$1-e^{-ta|\omega|^{-\zeta}}=G(\omega(at)^{-1/\zeta})$.
\end{proof}

Part (b) is an idealisation: the label law is not uniform, and $\hat k$ is a power law
only at high frequency (Laplace kernel: $\zeta=2$; Mat\'ern-$3/2$: $\zeta=4$; Gaussian:
exponential decay, $\zeta=\infty$). We therefore compute \eqref{eq:kgf} exactly on the
actual EXP-1 training sets ($\rho_h$ by 15-point Gauss--Hermite quadrature around each
label, three seeds, $\ell\in\{0.3,1\}\times\mathrm{sd}(y)$) and apply the estimator
\eqref{eq:heff} at the 20 conditions (\texttt{theory\_t2\_resolution.py},
Figure~\ref{fig:t2}). Three findings. \emph{The model is a Nadaraya--Watson mixture at
one bandwidth at every $t$}: under the Laplace kernel the median log-space $R^2$ of the
fit is $0.97$ and $h_{\mathrm{mean}}$ and $h_{\mathrm{eff}}$ differ by a median $11\%$
(Mat\'ern: $0.95$, $9\%$), as for the trained networks. \emph{$h_{\mathrm{eff}}$ falls to
$h$}, in 6/6 Laplace and 5/6 Mat\'ern configurations, as (a) predicts for $h=0$.
\emph{The rate is set by the spectrum}: $s(t)$ falls with log-log slope $-0.40$
(Laplace; $-1/\zeta=-0.5$) and $-0.29$ (Mat\'ern; $-0.25$), while under the Gaussian
kernel it barely moves ($-0.05$) and $h_{\mathrm{eff}}$ never reaches $h$ (0/6).

\paragraph{From moments to the field.} The model above acts on moments. At the level of
the field, a learner that resolves the label only to the law $\varphi$ of a perturbation
$u$ replaces $\vstar$ by its label average $v_\varphi$, and Proposition~\ref{prop:filtered} says that this keeps the atoms.

\begin{proposition}[Label resolution reweights the atoms and never moves them]
\label{prop:filtered}
Let $h>0$, $\varphi$ a probability measure on $\R^k$ and
$v_\varphi(x,t,y)=\int\vstar(x,t,y-u)\,\varphi(du)$. (a) $v_\varphi=\sum_i\tilde
w_i(x,t,y)(x^i-x)/(1-t)$ with $\tilde w_i\ge0$, $\sum_i\tilde w_i=1$, and $\tilde
w_i(x,0,y)=q_i(y):=\int p_i^{(h)}(y-u)\,\varphi(du)$. (b) If a trajectory of $v_\varphi$
converges as $t\to1$ to a point with a unique nearest training atom, that point is the
atom. Hence if $\pi_0$-almost every trajectory converges to such a point, the endpoint
law of $v_\varphi$ is $\sum_i\tilde q_i(y)\delta_{x^i}$ for some weights $\tilde q(y)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:filtered}]
\label{apx:pf-filtered}
(a) By the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:endpoint}, $\vstar(x,t,y')=\sum_iw_i(x,t,y')(x^i-x)/(1-t)$
with $w_i=a_ib_i/\sum_ja_jb_j$, $a_i=\pi_0(\frac{x-tx^i}{1-t})$, $b_i=K_h(y'-y^i)$;
averaging over $y'=y-u$ gives $\tilde w_i=\int w_i(x,t,y-u)\varphi(du)$, which is
nonnegative and sums to one. At $t=0$ all $a_i$ equal $\pi_0(x)$, so $w_i=p_i^{(h)}(y')$.
(b) Let $x_t\to\bar x$, with $x^i$ the unique nearest atom to $\bar x$ and
$\gamma=\min_{j\ne i}(|\bar x-x^j|^2-|\bar x-x^i|^2)>0$. For $t$ close to $1$,
$|x_t-tx^j|^2-|x_t-tx^i|^2\ge\gamma/2$, so
$a_j/a_i\le e^{-\gamma/(4(1-t)^2)}\to0$. Since $w_j\le\min\{1,(a_j/a_i)(b_j/b_i)\}$ and
$b_i>0$ everywhere, dominated convergence gives $\tilde w_j(x_t,t,y)\to0$ for $j\ne i$,
so $m_t:=\sum_j\tilde w_jx^j\to x^i$. Along the trajectory
$\dot x_t=(m_t-x_t)/(1-t)$ with $m_t-x_t\to x^i-\bar x$. If $x^i\ne\bar x$, then
$(x^i-\bar x)\cdot\dot x_t\ge|x^i-\bar x|^2/(2(1-t))$ for $t$ near $1$, whose integral
diverges, contradicting convergence. So $\bar x=x^i$.
\end{proof}

So a learner whose only defect is label resolution reweights the training atoms and
never leaves them; leaving them, as $38\%$ of CIFAR-10 samples do at $h{=}6$, needs an
error in the spatial dependence of the field. Integrating the flow of $v_\varphi$ exactly
on the EXP-1 training set (Gaussian $\varphi$ of scale $s$, five conditions, 300
trajectories each; \texttt{theory\_t2\_filtered.py}) confirms that every endpoint is an
atom (distance $\le0.0032$). The endpoint weights are \emph{not} simply the label-averaged
weights $q$: they agree within Monte Carlo error when $s\le h$ (total variation $0.11$
and $0.14$ against floors $0.09$ and $0.13$ at $s=h=0.05$ and $0.1$), but for $s\gg h$
the flow re-concentrates them, halving the endpoint variance ($0.46$ against $1.14$ at
$h=0.01$, $s=0.05$). A label-resolution limit is therefore not equivalent to extra label
noise at the level of the field, and the additive law has no reason to be exact.

The model leaves two things open. Its additive exponent is $p\approx2.2$ (Laplace; $2.8$
Mat\'ern; $2.8$ for the label-averaged weights $q$), against $p=1.3$ fitted to the networks, but the network data hardly
distinguish the two (log RMSE $0.352$ at $p=1.3$ against $0.366$ at $p=2$). And it
predicts no floor, whereas $h_{\mathrm{eff}}$ settles at $1.08h$ on the synthetic runs;
whether that gap is optimisation (Adam, a finite learning rate) or feature learning,
which kernel gradient flow excludes, is not settled here. Nor does kernel time map to
iterations outside the lazy regime, so we do not compare rates with training curves.

\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.94\textwidth]{fig_t2_resolution.png}
\caption{Kernel gradient flow \eqref{eq:kgf} on the EXP-1 training set (seed 0,
$\ell=\mathrm{sd}(y)$). (a) $s(t)$, the effective bandwidth at $h=0$: power-law decay
with the slope of Proposition~\ref{prop:specbias}(b) (dotted: $-1/\zeta$) for kernels
with power-law spectra, stagnation for the Gaussian kernel. (b) Under the Laplace
kernel $h_{\mathrm{eff}}$ falls and converges to each training bandwidth $h$ (dashed).}
